Abstract  30 
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 introduced the term �Community Profiles� to 31 reflect the use of the CSF for developing use case-specific cybersecurity risk management 32 guidance for multiple organizations. This guide provides considerations for creating and using 33 Community Profiles to help implement the Framework. The guide describes Community 34 Profiles, provides guidance for the content that may be conveyed through a Community Profile, 35 and offers a Community Profile Lifecycle (Plan, Develop, Use, Maintain). 36 
Keywords 37 
Community Profiles; cybersecurity; Cybersecurity Framework (CSF); cybersecurity risk 38 governance; cybersecurity risk management; enterprise risk management; Profiles. 39 
Audience 40 
The primary audience for this guide is communities, which are groups of organizations with 41 shared interests in cybersecurity risk management within a specific context, such as a sector, 42 technology, or challenge, that are interested in developing one or more Community Profiles. 43

e the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) was first released in 2014, the CSF has been used 76 by communities with shared interests in cybersecurity risk management. These communities 77 developed what are now called �Community Profiles� to outline shared interests, goals, and 78 outcomes within a specific context, such as a sector, technology, or challenge. CSF 2.0 79 introduced the term �Community Profiles� to describe the ways various organizations have 80 used CSF Profiles to develop cybersecurity risk management guidance that applies to multiple 81 organizations, as well as to differentiate them from Organizational Profiles that are internally 82 focused on the organization itself and generally not shared publicly. A Community Profile can 83 be thought of as guidance for a specific community that is organized around the common 84 taxonomy of the CSF. 85 
This guide provides considerations for creating and using Community Profiles to implement the 86 CSF 2.0. This guide is intended to provide a starting point, as there are a myriad of ways that 87 Community Profiles have been developed to serve communities. 1. About Community Profiles 91 
A Community Profile describes shared interests, goals, and outcomes for reducing 92 cybersecurity risk among a number of organizations. Community Profiles provide a way for 93 communities to reflect a consensus point of view about cybersecurity risk management. 94 Organizations in the community can use a Community Profile as the basis of, or to inform, their 95 Organizational Target Profiles. Some communities may develop more than one Community 96 Profile, based on the scope of their needs. 97 
Communities are organizations that share a common context and an interest in their 98 cybersecurity posture. Examples of communities that a Community Profile may support include: 99 
� Sectors/subsectors (e.g., critical infrastructure sectors) 100 

� Technologies (e.g., mobile, cloud) 101 

� Other use cases (e.g., thwarting ransomware attacks) 102

 Benefits  113 
Community Profiles offer a variety of potential benefits, including: 114 
� Describing a shared taxonomy for cybersecurity risk management and priorities in the 115 context of the community 116 

� Encouraging common target outcomes that organizations within the community can use 117 to inform their assessments of cybersecurity progress 118 

� Aligning requirements from multiple sources under one framework 119 

� Leveraging expertise across the community 120 

� Minimizing the burden for each organization by providing priorities and outcomes that 121 organizations can use to develop their own Target Profiles 122 


The benefits communities will find most valuable shape how they scope and approach 123 developing their Community Profile(s). 124

The Community Profile developer should have community 128 expertise, capabilities to convene other experts that represent the interests of the community, 129 and resources to support development. Examples of organizations that may collaboratively 130 develop and maintain Community Profiles include trade associations, nonprofit entities, 131 government agencies, advisory committees, and information sharing organizations. A large 132 organization with distinct operational components might even develop a Community Profile for 133 internal use across its divisions or units. 134 
2. Community Profiles Contents 135 
Community Profiles use the CSF Core to highlight and prioritize cybersecurity outcomes that are 136 important for achieving community priorities. A Community Profile provides information that 137 enables the community to make risk-informed decisions when determining how to use its 138 cybersecurity resources. 139

3. The Community Profile Lifecycle 170 
 171 
Fig. 2: Community Profile Lifestyle 172 
Fig. 2 illustrates the Community Profile Lifecycle. Developing a Community Profile begins with a 173 planning process that includes understanding the needs of the community it is intended to 174 support and determining the scope of the Profile. Thoughtful planning enables the 175 development process, resulting in the Community Profile. The Profile is then ready for use by 176 organizations in the community. Community Profiles are reviewed periodically and updated as 177 needed to ensure they are adequately maintained and continue to meet the needs of the 178 community or are retired when no longer needed. 179

Most Community Profiles are intended to address many roles, from 193 directors and executive leaders to hands-on implementers. 194 2. Scope the Profile. The Profile�s scope should be broad enough to accommodate the 195 variety of community members but not so broad that it does not adequately capture the 196 community�s cybersecurity needs. Some communities also determine whether the 197 Community Profile will be a voluntary resource or will be required for the community. 198

Aligning community priorities 199 requires participation of knowledgeable experts across the community with a variety of 200 operational experience in addition to cybersecurity experts. Integrating Other NIST Frameworks 223 
While a CSF Community Profile can be a valuable tool on its own, 224 communities may consider integrating other related or complementary 225 frameworks, such as the NIST Privacy Framework, NIST (cybersecurity) 226 Risk Management Framework (RMF), or NIST Artificial Intelligence (AI) 227 RMF. Additionally, incorporating links to other resources, such as the 228 NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity (NICE Framework) or NIST 229 Privacy Workforce Taxonomy, may help communities with identifying 230 work roles and aligning staff to implement prioritized Subcategories in 231 the Community Profile.  232

After planning a Community Profile, follow these steps to develop it:  235 
1. Identify community priorities and objectives. While each organization within a 236 community has its own mission objectives and priorities, there are common or universal 237 interests that support the community. Community Profile teams begin with identifying 238 these universal priorities, which describe the fundamental purposes, operations, or use 239 cases of a community. 240 


Questions to ask that may help the community identify its shared priorities include: 241 
� How would you describe the purpose of the community? 242 

� What are the critical activities in the community and why are they important? 243 

� What are the current risk management requirements the community must 244 adhere to? 245 

� Are there current community opportunities or priorities to include? 246 

� Are there any dependencies outside the community? 247 

� What are the threats to the success of the community? 248 

� What are the key assets that support each priority? 249

Once the priorities are agreed upon, the community may decide to rank the priorities in 252 order of relative importance. This helps organizations within the community make 253 strategic planning decisions. 254 
2. Align community priorities with CSF outcomes. Once community priorities are 255 identified, the development team aligns those priorities with the CSF outcomes that 256 enable or support them. Communities can choose a simple prioritization schema (e.g., 257 Included/Not Included) or a multi-level schema (e.g., High, Moderate, Implement Later) 258 to provide more insights when creating a gap analysis or action plan. Inputs for adding 259 and prioritizing outcomes include community-specific Informative References, shared 260 threats in the community, inputs from community experts, and other resources that the 261 community finds beneficial. 262 3. Fill out the Profile. There is no required format for a Community Profile. Some 263 communities use a narrative format with prose and tables. O

262 3. Fill out the Profile. There is no required format for a Community Profile. Some 263 communities use a narrative format with prose and tables. Others prefer a table format 264 that can be manipulated and sorted in a variety of ways. Still others prefer a format that 265 can be ingested into and manipulated by governance tools. 266 


Development teams can capitalize on existing resources rather than creating the 267 Community Profile from a virtual blank page. For example, some communities may 268 already have a set of priorities or community-specific cybersecurity standards. 269 
Also, the NIST National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE) has published 270 multiple Community Profiles that can be used as examples of additional narrative 271 discussions that may be included along with the basic Community Profile contents 272 described in Section 2. Published Community Profiles are available on the NCCoE 273 Framework Resource Center. 274

Community Profiles can serve as valuable tools for assessing both the 302 community and organizations within the community. At the community 303 level, Profiles can help a community determine where its ecosystem has 304 systemic cybersecurity challenges and work in collaboration

In addition to using Community Profiles to create an Organizational 307 Target Profile, organizations can use the information in Community 308 Profiles to inform how they conduct internal assessments of their 309 progress in relation to community expectations. Communities may 310 choose to include assessment criteria and implementation examples to 311 facilitate consistent evaluation by community members.
